During a spring journey down the Volga, the frail, deeply religious Mitia helps steer his father Silan’s raft alongside the hired laborer Sergei. Sergei relentlessly mocks Mitia because Silan is openly having an affair with Mitia’s wife, Marka. Mitia explains that he never wanted the marriage and refused to live with Marka as her husband, believing intimacy without love would violate his conscience. Feeling rejected and ruined, Marka turned to the vigorous, domineering Silan.

Mitia insists that true law lies within the soul and dreams of escaping his corrupt family to join a persecuted Christian brotherhood in the Caucasus. Sergei initially treats the scandal as a joke and blames Mitia’s weakness for creating it, but his taunts eventually drive Mitia into a sobbing collapse. Mitia begs to be left alone, warning that the torment may make him throw himself into the river. Sergei finally grasps the depth of his suffering and becomes uneasy.

At the front of the raft, Silan and Marka embrace and discuss their situation. Silan admits their relationship is sinful but claims their love justifies the risk. He regrets arranging Marka’s marriage to Mitia shortly before his own wife died, since otherwise he could have married her lawfully. Bitterly contemptuous of his son’s weakness, Silan imagines that Mitia’s death would free them to marry, move far away, and atone through good works. Marka prays that the sickly Mitia will die soon. As dawn clears the clouds and brightens the river, the raft continues downstream, with Mitia still trapped between his spiritual convictions, public humiliation, and his father’s overpowering will.

The story uses a strongly naturalistic, psychologically charged realist style, enriched by lyrical landscape description and symbolic contrasts. Its prose alternates between expansive, atmospheric narration and coarse, energetic dialogue, placing private moral conflict against the immense physical presence of the Volga. The result is both socially observant and melodramatically intense: the characters belong to a specific peasant and working world, but their dispute is framed as a larger struggle between bodily vitality, spiritual conscience, custom, desire, and power.

The narrative voice is third-person and broadly omniscient. It moves freely from external observation into interpretive commentary, explaining not only what characters do but what their voices, gestures, and silences reveal about them. The narrator frequently assigns emotional or metaphysical significance to physical details: Silan’s shouting expresses his surplus of strength, Sergei’s need to talk is presented as resistance to the oppressive silence, and Mitia’s physical weakness mirrors his inward torment. Characterization is therefore overt rather than reticent. Epithets and compact descriptive labels—“fair, weak, melancholy-looking,” “bluff, healthy, red-bearded,” “energetic, tall, mocking”—establish moral and temperamental contrasts immediately.

Landscape is the dominant stylistic instrument. The river, fog, clouds, darkness, moonlight, and eventual sunrise are repeatedly personified and made responsive to the human drama. Water “wails,” stillness “suffocates,” clouds “bar the way,” the night possesses a “hidden meditative silence,” and nature later “thrilled, quickened, and smiled.” The opening’s gray, oppressive world externalizes Mitia’s entrapment and shame, while the clearing sky and richly colored dawn accompany Silan and Marka’s confident affirmation of desire. This correspondence is not simply decorative: nature acts as an emotional chorus. Recurring images of walls, crushing vapor, fathomless water, wolves, fire, and strangling nooses give the story a symbolic vocabulary of obstruction, predation, torment, and doom.

The descriptive diction is elevated, sensuous, and often painterly. Color is carefully controlled, progressing from “ragged gray,” “gray-black,” “humid,” and “leaden” to yellow moonlight, polished steel, purple-gold waves, emerald fields, and “dew diamonds.” Sound is equally important. Onomatopoeic and auditory phrases such as “wistful wailing swish,” “thud-thud,” “groaned and scraped,” “gurgled musically,” and repeated cries of “Ahoy!” make the raft’s world physically immediate. Silence is treated almost as a substance, repeatedly broken by engines, laughter, curses, sobbing, or powerful male voices. The opposition between silence and sound parallels the opposition between Mitia’s inwardness and the other men’s forceful appetite for life.

Sentence structure varies according to mode. Landscape passages favor long, cumulative sentences with participial phrases, coordinated clauses, semicolons, dashes, and repeated modifiers. These sentences create a slow, drifting rhythm analogous to clouds, fog, and the raft’s movement. Short declarative sentences—“The raft floats onward,” “Day broke gradually,” “The water murmured”—punctuate the flow and give scenic transitions a grave simplicity. Dialogue, by contrast, is rapid, fragmented, and exclamatory. It contains interruptions, repetitions, rhetorical questions, curses, imperatives, colloquialisms, and abrupt tonal shifts. Sergei’s speech in particular sprawls through taunts and improvised arguments, while Mitia’s language moves from hesitant, conciliatory phrasing into biblical denunciation and ecstatic religious cadence.

The dialogue is the chief means of social and psychological revelation. Sergei speaks in a rough, mocking vernacular full of insults, proverbial formulations, and bodily metaphors: a man must have “teeth and claws,” Mitia is “neither fish nor fowl,” and his thoughts are treated as a useless “maggot.” His teasing is repetitive and performative; he talks partly to dominate Mitia and partly to fend off silence and loneliness. Mitia’s speech is quieter, abstract, and religious, centered on “soul,” “law,” “God,” “sin,” and “Christ.” At emotional peaks it becomes sermon-like, using parallel clauses, anaphora, apostrophe, and scriptural imagery: the others are “wolves,” “beasts,” and men “rending each other’s flesh.” Silan’s speech is blunt, possessive, and decisive, combining awareness of sin with an unapologetic ethic of strength and passionate living. Marka speaks less and is rendered more through looks, posture, smiles, and physical responsiveness than through extended argument.

The characterization is organized through stark contrasts. Mitia is pale, sickly, passive, introspective, and spiritually absolutist; Silan is physically powerful, sexually vigorous, socially authoritative, and pleased with his own vitality. Sergei occupies an unstable middle position: he admires strength and ridicules weakness, yet he is also lonely, envious, curious, and eventually unsettled by the suffering he has provoked. Bodies carry ideological meaning throughout. Expanded chests, hairy arms, powerful throats, strong teeth, bare feet, and steel-spring muscles signify fitness for the harsh material world, whereas coughing, panting, thin hands, sobbing, and collapse identify Mitia’s inability to inhabit that world on its terms. This emphasis gives the prose a pronounced naturalistic determinism, even while Mitia argues for spiritual freedom.

The pacing alternates between suspended scenic description and escalating verbal confrontation. The raft’s steady downstream movement provides continuity, but the action itself is comparatively limited: steering, passing a steamer, talking, embracing, and watching dawn arrive. Dramatic momentum comes from gradual disclosure. Sergei’s teasing first reveals the father’s relationship with Marka, then Mitia explains his rejection of marriage, then his religious plan to flee, and finally his shame erupts into a breakdown. The chapter division shifts perspective forward to Silan and Marka, replaying the same moral conflict from the lovers’ side. This creates dramatic irony and complicates judgment: Silan and Marka know they are sinning, yet regard their love as vital and authentic, while Mitia’s moral purity has also helped create the situation.

Repetition is a major rhetorical feature. Words and concepts such as “soul,” “sin,” “law,” “strength,” “silence,” “darkness,” and “life” recur insistently. Characters repeat questions and commands—“How did it happen?”, “Get married!”, “Give her up!”, “Look ahead!”—until they become emotional refrains. “Look ahead” has both a practical and symbolic resonance: the men must navigate the river, but each is also trying, or failing, to imagine a future. The raft itself functions as a confined dramatic stage on which incompatible people are bound together and carried onward by a force larger than themselves.

The tone combines tragic seriousness, harsh comedy, sensual admiration, and moral ambiguity. Sergei’s mockery can be comic in rhythm and phrasing, but it repeatedly crosses into cruelty. Silan and Marka’s erotic warmth is rendered with sympathy and physical vividness, yet their wish for Mitia’s death introduces menace. Mitia is treated compassionately, though his idealism is also shown as impractical, self-denying, and implicated in the suffering of others. The prose does not offer a simple moral verdict. Instead, it sets competing laws against one another: religious conscience, social custom, masculine power, sexual need, paternal authority, and individual love.

The story bears the marks of an older English translation. There are formal or archaic constructions, heavy punctuation, conspicuous explanatory narration, occasional typographical or grammatical irregularities, and idioms such as “rum un,” “bad ’un,” “I’m blest,” and “king of trumps,” which give Russian peasant speech a distinctly period English coloring. Exclamation marks and dashes are abundant, and emotions are often named explicitly. The editorial footnote supplies sociological and historical explanation from outside the fictional scene, a practice characteristic of older translated editions. Overall, the style is robust, elemental, and high-contrast: lyrical nature writing surrounds a raw spoken drama, while physical detail and symbolic atmosphere transform a peasant family scandal into a conflict between life-force and conscience.

# THE LAW WITHIN

## I

The raft floated down the Volga.

All night the river had lain under a ragged gray covering of clouds, and now, toward morning, the clouds had descended so low that they seemed to rest upon the black crests of the wooded banks and to drag their wet bellies across the water. The river was scarcely visible. It appeared and vanished between strips of fog—here dull as lead, there polished like old steel, and farther away swallowed altogether by the humid darkness. The piled timber of the raft groaned, scraped, and trembled; the water, divided by its broad snout, went away on either side with a wistful wailing swish, as though complaining that this rude, clumsy thing had broken the hidden meditative silence of the night.

At the stern stood three men.

Silan, the owner of the timber and master of the raft, held the steering sweep beneath his arm. He was a broad, tall peasant of five-and-fifty, bluff, healthy, red-bearded, with a chest like the front of a blacksmith’s shop and hands so large that the wooden handle looked slender in them. His shirt was open at the throat; wet red hair covered the powerful neck and breast, and whenever he shouted an order the sound rolled over the water with the abundance of a strength which must spend itself in noise, labour, anger, or love.

Beside him worked Sergei, the hired man—a long-legged fellow of thirty, lean in the hips, broad in the shoulders, with a pointed beard and quick, mocking eyes. His bare feet gripped the damp logs as if they had claws. He was never silent for long. Silence oppressed him. In it he became conscious of the fog, the fathomless water, the dark banks, his own poverty, and the unpleasant fact that there were no people near to laugh at his jokes. Therefore he talked, whistled, cursed the river, hailed invisible fishermen, and teased whoever stood nearest.

The third was Mitia, Silan’s son.

He was fair, weak, melancholy-looking, and scarcely seemed to belong either to the strong raft or to the mighty river beneath it. Though nearly twenty-seven, he had the narrow shoulders and smooth, tired face of a sickly lad. A pale beard, fine as dried grass, grew upon his cheeks; his blue eyes were large and uncertain; his thin fingers, wound about the sweep, reddened under the strain. From time to time he coughed, bending his head, and after each cough he looked ashamed, as though even his illness were an offence to the healthy men beside him.

“Pull, you sleepy saints!” Silan roared. “Pull to port! Do you want the bank in our teeth?”

The three leaned against the steering sweep. The massive blade groaned in the current. Loose ropes creaked; water gurgled musically between the timbers.

“Harder!” shouted Silan. “Mitia! Have you fallen asleep standing?”

“I am pulling,” answered Mitia.

“Pull with your bones, then, if you’ve no flesh!”

Sergei laughed.

“That’s right, master! Warm him up. A fellow such as he needs fire under his heels. He lives as if he were asking pardon of the earth for walking on it.”

Mitia said nothing. They brought the raft round, avoiding a low, mist-covered spit of sand, and the river once more seized them and drew them onward. Silan planted the sweep, glanced ahead, and then strode over the logs toward the forward hut.

His heavy steps went thud-thud, thud-thud, diminishing in the fog.

Sergei looked after him and winked at Mitia.

“There goes a man!” he said. “Eh? A real man, your father. He need only stamp and the ground remembers it. Whereas you—Lord save us!—you could fall out of heaven and not bend a blade of grass.”

Mitia kept his eyes upon the water.

“Look ahead,” he said quietly.

“I am looking. There’s fog ahead, fog behind, fog inside your skull. Nothing else. Ah, Mitia, Mitia! How did the Almighty contrive it? Such an oak of a father, and from his acorn—this little mushroom!”

“Do your work, Sergei.”

“I am doing it. My tongue does not hinder my hands. A working man has two hands and one tongue, and all three must earn their bread. Besides, if I keep quiet, I begin to think. Thinking’s a bad maggot—it gnaws holes in a poor man. Better talk.”

Mitia’s thin shoulders rose and fell.

“Then talk of something else.”

“Why? Is this not interesting? It is a wonder fit for a fair booth. ‘Come and see, honest Christians! The husband steers at the stern while his wife lies warm at the bow with his father!’ Ha!”

Mitia turned his face toward Sergei. Even in the uncertain grayness it was possible to see the blood rise under his pale skin.

“Don’t.”

“One kopeck admission! Children half-price! The father’s young, the son’s old; the husband fasts, the father feasts—”

“Enough.”

Sergei grinned, pleased by the success of his words. Until that instant he had only desired amusement. He did not hate Mitia. Indeed, he bore him the obscure resentment which a vigorous but dependent man often bears toward one weaker than himself who possesses property, a name, and the right to call the master father. Yet there was also curiosity in his mockery, and even envy. The scandal had warmth in it. It glowed before his imagination like a house fire in winter, and he wished continually to come nearer, to thrust in his hands, to see who would be burned.

“Why enough? It’s true.”

“Truth can be sinful in the mouth.”

“Oh-ho! Hear the preacher! Then a lie may be holy, perhaps?”

“Yes. Sometimes silence is holier than truth.”

“Silence! There’s your king of trumps. Whenever life catches you by the collar—silence! When your wife calls you—silence! When your father takes her—silence! If a wolf bit off your leg, you’d say, ‘Brother wolf, let us not discuss it.’”

Mitia closed his eyes for a moment.

Far in the mist a steamer gave a deep hoarse cry. It sounded not like a machine but like some enormous blind beast wandering between the banks and calling for its mate.

“Ah-oy!” Silan shouted from the front.

“Ah-oy!” answered Sergei with delight.

The steamer’s paddle-wheels struck the water: thud-thud, thud-thud, nearer and louder. A yellow light came swimming through the fog, grew into two fiery eyes, and passed across the river. Then the dark bulk of the vessel emerged, streaming moisture. Men’s voices rang from its deck; a bell clanged; sparks flew from the funnel and died over the black water. For a minute the river awakened into movement and sound. The raft rocked on the waves; ropes snapped taut; the hut creaked; water splashed over Mitia’s feet.

Sergei waved his cap.

“Ahoy, you devils! Take us with you!”

Someone on the steamer whistled shrilly. Laughter answered from the darkness, and then the vessel passed. Its red stern lamp diminished, trembling like a drop of blood, and the fog closed over it. The waves continued to run, lifting the raft and letting it fall with long, sleepy sighs.

When silence returned, it seemed heavier than before.

Sergei spat into the water.

“There! People are travelling, eating, drinking, kissing the girls in the cabins. And we creep on logs through soup thick enough for a spoon. Talk, Mitia.”

“I have nothing to say.”

“You have a wife.”

Mitia’s hands tightened on the sweep.

“Do not speak of her.”

“Why not? She’s handsome. Dark eyes, red mouth, hips like a mare—”

“Be quiet!”

The cry was sharp but weak. Sergei looked at him and chuckled.

“Ah! So there is blood in you. I thought it was holy water. If you cannot bear another man to praise her, why did you send her from your bed?”

“I did not send her.”

“No? She ran of herself?”

“I never called her.”

“Same thing. Worse, perhaps. Tell me, Mitia—between ourselves, like Christian men—what happened? Your father married you, the priest sang, the people drank, she took off her boots and sat on your bed. Then what? Did you read her a psalm?”

Mitia moved away, but the sweep held them together.

“You know nothing.”

“Then teach me. I am ignorant. Was she not willing?”

“She was willing.”

“And you?”

“I could not.”

Sergei whistled.

“Could not! There’s a word! A young wife, warm from the wedding, and he could not. Were you ill?”

“No.”

“Frightened?”

“No.”

“Then what?”

Mitia looked ahead. The fog had formed a wall across the river, smooth, dense, and gray-black. The raft seemed to be travelling toward that wall and could never reach it. Behind them, their wake disappeared almost at once; thus they were cut off from what had been and barred from what might be, imprisoned upon a few wet logs between vapor and water.

“I did not love her,” Mitia said.

Sergei waited; then laughed so loudly that the fog returned a faint broken echo.

“Did not love her! Oh, I’m blest! Must a cock love every grain he pecks? She was your wife.”

“That is why.”

“What is why?”

“Because she was my wife I could not deceive her. If I had taken her without love, I should have used her body and lied to her soul. The priest’s words could not make that clean.”

Sergei scratched his beard.

“Wait. You were married before God.”

“Before men.”

“Before God too. There were icons.”

“Icons do not answer for us.”

“The priest blessed you.”

“The priest is not my conscience.”

“Well, then!” Sergei’s voice grew triumphant, as if he had caught a thief. “You set yourself above the priest, above the Church, above your father—above God, perhaps?”

“No. Under God.”

Mitia spoke softly, but something stubborn entered his voice. It was the stubbornness of a thin root which, unable to overthrow a rock, nevertheless grows crookedly round it and lives.

“There is a law written inside us,” he continued. “Not on paper, not in books, not in the mouth of a priest who has eaten too much, but in the soul. A man may obey every custom and yet be filthy before God. He may break a custom and be pure.”

Sergei stared at him.

“What law says a man must leave his wife untouched?”

“The law that forbids a lie.”

“A lie! You’d not have been lying. You’d have been lying beside her.”

He laughed at his own joke, slapped his thigh, and nearly slipped on the wet timber.

Mitia bent his head.

“You make dirt of everything.”

“Because everything comes out of dirt. We’re born in blood, eat from the earth, sweat in work, rot underground. What else are we? Angels? Have you wings beneath your shirt?”

“We are souls.”

“We are stomachs first. Ask a hungry man.”

“No. A beast is stomach first.”

“And a man without stomach is dead. Listen to me, Mitia. God gave a man teeth and claws—”

“We have no claws.”

“Then he gave us fists! Look at your father’s. A man must bite life before life bites him. He must take a wife, give her children, earn money, fight when struck, shout when wronged. He must stand. You don’t stand. You hang from the world like an empty sleeve.”

Mitia’s face contracted. He breathed heavily through his mouth.

Sergei, who felt himself becoming eloquent, leaned closer.

“And now what? You would not be a husband, so another man became one. A woman is not an icon to wait in a corner while you pray. She has blood. She has arms that want holding, a breast that wants a child. Marka was married, but she lived like a widow. Your father—well, your father is no widow.”

“Stop.”

“He looked at her. She looked at him. Fire knows dry straw. Who is to blame?”

“I am,” Mitia whispered.

Sergei had expected denial, and this answer momentarily checked him.

“There! You know it.”

“I am to blame for consenting to the marriage. I told father I did not wish it. He shouted. He said she was strong, good, from decent people; he said a wife would cure me of thinking. I gave way. That was my sin.”

“And afterward?”

“I asked her forgiveness.”

“What did she say?”

Mitia’s lips moved before any sound came.

“She wept.”

“And then?”

“She asked if she were ugly. I said no. She asked if there were another woman. I said no. She asked if I hated her. I said no. She said, ‘Then why?’ I tried to explain.”

Sergei shook his head with grim amusement.

“You explained the soul to a bride in bed.”

“I told her that my heart was not joined to hers, and that the body must not go where the heart cannot follow.”

“Oho!”

“She did not understand.”

“Naturally.”

“She thought I was laughing at her. The next day she would not look at me. After a week she called me a dead man. Then father began to quarrel with me. He said I had disgraced him. He struck me.”

“Didn’t you strike back?”

“He is my father.”

“There again! Always a fine reason for doing nothing.”

The clouds shifted slowly. Through a rent in them the moon showed itself, swollen and yellow, looking down upon the river with a sick, unfriendly face. Its light spread in a narrow road over the water, and in that road the waves moved like scales upon an enormous serpent. For a few moments Mitia’s face became clear—his hollow cheeks, moist eyes, and the bluish shadow beneath them. Sergei saw that he looked older than his father.

“And Marka?” he asked, more quietly.

“She became hard. Shame made her hard. When people began to whisper, she laughed so that they should think she did not care. Father defended her. He scolded me before her. They stood together, and I—”

“You what?”

“I went away.”

“To where?”

“The shed. The fields. The church porch. Anywhere.”

“And left them together?”

“I did not know then.”

Sergei gave a contemptuous snort.

“You did not know because you would not see. A blind man at least feels with a stick. You shut your eyes and called it holiness.”

Mitia flinched as if the words had struck him.

From the forward part of the raft came Silan’s voice, speaking indistinctly, then a woman’s low laugh. The sound was scarcely louder than the gurgling water, yet both men heard it. Sergei’s quick eyes turned toward Mitia.

Mitia stood rigid.

Marka laughed again.

It was a warm, full laugh, not merry so much as contented, and amid the chill vapor it seemed improper and splendid, like a red flower opening in a graveyard.

Sergei rubbed his nose.

“She does not sound unhappy now.”

Mitia breathed out slowly.

“No.”

“Your father has cured her.”

Mitia’s lower lip trembled.

“Sergei, in God’s name—”

“What? I only say—”

“In God’s name, leave me.”

Sergei was uneasy for an instant, but he could not abandon the jest. To withdraw would have seemed like defeat, and he had the cruel instinct, common in strong animals and heedless men, to press upon whatever recoils.

“Come, don’t sour yourself! There is an easy cure. Give her up openly. Let your father marry her.”

“She is my wife.”

“Now she is your wife! A moment ago the priest and paper meant nothing.”

“A bond can be sinful and still bind.”

“That’s twisted rope indeed. Then take her back.”

“No.”

“Beat your father.”

“No.”

“Go to the magistrate.”

“No.”

“Run away.”

“Yes.”

Sergei blinked.

“Where?”

“To the Caucasus.”

“The Caucasus! What for?”

“There are brethren there.”

“What brethren?”

“Christians.”

“We are Christians here.”

Mitia looked at him, and in his eyes there appeared a strange, distant brightness.

“No. Here men cross themselves, then rend one another’s flesh. They bow to painted boards, then sell the poor for profit. They call killing lawful if a uniform orders it, marriage holy if a drunken priest blesses it, and greed respectable if the thief has land. Those are not Christians.”

Sergei glanced toward the front of the raft.

“Speak lower. Your father will hear.”

“What if he does?”

“He’ll pitch your Christianity into the river.”

“He has beaten me before.”

“And these brethren—what are they? Sectarians?”

“They follow Christ’s law. They will not bear arms. They will not swear oaths. They own all things in common. They feed the hungry and call no man master.”

“Then how do they live?”

“By work.”

Sergei laughed again, but less heartily.

“Every fool says that before dinner. After dinner he finds a master. And they’ll take you?”

“If God leads me.”

“Can you plough?”

“I can learn.”

“Fell timber?”

“I can learn.”

“Carry a sack?”

“I will carry what strength permits.”

“Strength!” Sergei seized Mitia’s wrist and held it up. “Look at that! A goose’s neck. The Caucasus has mountains, not feather beds. You’ll cough once climbing a hill and roll down dead.”

“Then I shall die among brethren.”

“Why not die at home? It’s cheaper.”

“Because here there is no air.”

Sergei looked around at the immense river, the moving fog, the unseen spaces beyond the banks.

“No air! There’s enough to drown in.”

“Not for the soul.”

Again Marka’s voice sounded ahead, but the words were lost. Silan answered, and his deep laugh rolled along the raft. Mitia shuddered.

Sergei saw it.

“Jealous after all,” he said.

Mitia shook his head.

“Don’t lie. Your belly twists when she laughs with him.”

“It is shame.”

“Jealousy.”

“Shame!”

“Call a dog a lamb and it still barks. You wanted her only when another took her.”

“No!”

Mitia pulled at his wrist, but Sergei held it. The hired man was smiling, and in the yellow moonlight his teeth showed strong and white beneath his pointed beard.

“Confess it. You dream of her now. At night you hear them through the wall. You lie there under your blanket, holy as a corpse, and listen—”

Mitia tore himself free.

“Be silent!”

His cry flew across the water. Silan’s voice stopped at the front. For several moments there was only the river.

Then Silan called:

“What are you barking about?”

“Nothing!” Sergei answered. “Mitia’s preaching to the fog!”

“Watch the channel!”

“We’re watching!”

Sergei turned, still grinning, but Mitia’s expression silenced him. The weak man seemed suddenly to have been drawn upward by an inward flame. His pale eyes shone; his hands shook; every tendon stood out in his neck.

“You think because I am weak you may tear me,” he said. “You all think so. Father thinks so. Marka thinks so. A wolf sees a lame creature and bites because it limps. You laugh and bite. You are strong, therefore everything is permitted you—is that your law?”

“Come now—”

“You speak of teeth, fists, blood! Beasts! All of you beasts, rending one another’s flesh and proud because your jaws are red! One takes money, another takes a woman, another takes a life. And afterward you cross yourselves and say: ‘It is custom. It is nature. It is lawful.’ Whose law? The wolf’s law!”

Sergei’s smile vanished.

“You’d best not call the master a wolf.”

“He is a wolf. My father is a wolf. He brought Marka into our house for me when I begged him not to. He fastened us together like two dogs and beat me because we would not mate. Then he desired her himself. Now he walks before me, eats before me, lies with my wife, and shouts that I am weak. Yes, I am weak! Does that make his sin clean? Does strength turn filth into gold?”

“Keep your voice down.”

“And you—you follow him because you admire his shoulders. You laugh because his wickedness is lively and my suffering is dull. If I struck you, you would understand. If I bled, you would understand. But the soul bleeds without colour, and so you put your finger into the wound for sport.”

Sergei stepped back.

Mitia’s anger left him as quickly as it had come. His body bent; he grasped the sweep with both hands, not to guide it but to keep himself upright. A dry cough shook him. Then another. He tried to speak, coughed again, and suddenly began to sob.

There was nothing restrained or dignified in the sound. It burst from him in broken, childish gasps. His narrow shoulders jerked; his mouth opened helplessly; tears ran down his cheeks and hung upon the pale hairs of his beard. He hid his face against his sleeve.

Sergei stared in astonishment.

He had seen men cry when drunk, when flogged, when a horse died, or when a mother’s coffin was lowered; such tears were comprehensible and even respectable. But this naked collapse frightened him. It was as though, in tapping upon a thin wall for amusement, he had broken through and discovered behind it not a room but a black, bottomless pit.

“Oh, come,” he muttered. “That’s enough. I was joking.”

Mitia wept harder.

“Don’t,” said Sergei. “What are you doing? The master will hear.”

“Leave me,” Mitia gasped.

“I didn’t mean—well, I meant it, but not like that. A man talks. My tongue’s loose.”

“Leave me!”

“I can’t leave the sweep.”

“Then be silent. For God’s sake, be silent.”

Sergei shifted from one foot to the other.

“You mustn’t take words so deep. Words are wind.”

“They are nails.”

“A man cannot live if every fool’s word enters his heart.”

“I know.”

“Wipe your face. Come! Marka might come back.”

At her name Mitia uttered a strangled sound.

“Don’t say it.”

Sergei lowered his voice.

“All right.”

“Do not speak to me again tonight.”

“All right.”

“Because I cannot bear it.”

Sergei looked uneasily at the water slipping past. The moon had gone behind cloud once more, and the river was black, soft, and apparently without surface or bottom. Small whirlpools opened beside the raft, turned with oily deliberation, and disappeared.

Mitia too was looking at them.

“Do not torment me,” he whispered. “Sometimes, when you laugh, and he shouts, and she—when there is nowhere to go—I think the water is quiet underneath.”

Sergei’s scalp prickled.

“What nonsense.”

“It would close over me. No priest, no law, no father.”

“Stop that.”

“I know it is sin.”

“Then don’t think it.”

“Can a man command thoughts as he commands oxen?”

“You said the law was inside.”

“The law is there. Strength is not.”

Sergei gripped his shoulder.

“Listen! You’re not to jump. Do you hear?”

Mitia raised his wet face.

“You hurt me.”

Sergei released him at once.

“I only— You gave me a fright. A fellow says such things in darkness, on a river—what am I to think?”

“Think nothing. Be silent.”

They stood together at the stern, and for a long while neither spoke.

The raft floated onward.

The fog thinned in places. A dark bank appeared on the right, high and wooded, with birches standing ghostly among the pines. Somewhere beyond it a dog barked, faint and solitary. An answering dog called farther away; then another, until the sounds passed from village to village like watchmen handing along a warning. The river murmured. The logs scraped. A loose chain knocked softly against a ring—clink, clink, clink—with the patience of a clock measuring time for men who could neither hasten nor turn back.

Sergei watched Mitia from the corner of his eye.

The pale man had ceased sobbing, but tears still came silently. He steered correctly, almost mechanically. That frightened Sergei more than the weeping. He wished to say something kind, yet kindness was a language his tongue had scarcely learned. Every phrase that came to him sounded like a jest or command.

At last he muttered:

“When we reach Samara, I’ll buy you tea.”

Mitia did not answer.

“Hot tea,” Sergei added. “With sugar.”

Still no answer.

Sergei sighed. He looked ahead toward the low shelter where Silan and Marka were, and for the first time he did not envy the master. The raft seemed no longer a merry scandal but a trap made of timber, fog, flesh, and sin, bound with ropes too thick for any knife.

“Look ahead,” Mitia said suddenly.

Sergei started.

A black snag thrust from the water. Together they heaved on the sweep. The raft turned slowly, its flank missing the snag by a few feet. The current caught the timbers again and bore them into darkness.

## II

At the front of the raft, under an awning of sailcloth stretched beside the hut, Silan and Marka sat close together.

A lantern hung from a hook above them, but its flame had burned low and red. It threw an uncertain light upon coils of rope, an iron kettle, sacks of flour, and Silan’s heavy boots. Beyond the awning, fog streamed past in gray veils. The wet air smelled of pine resin, river mud, smoke, and the warm human bodies crowded beneath the canvas.

Marka was twenty-three, dark, handsome, full-bodied. Her black hair had come loose from beneath her kerchief and lay in a thick braid over one shoulder. She wore a red blouse, and although its colour had dulled in the lantern light, it seemed to hold warmth of its own. Her eyes, usually bold before other people, softened when she looked at Silan. Yet about her mouth there remained something wounded and defiant—the fixed trace left by months of humiliation, whispers, and resisted tears.

Silan had one arm around her. His broad palm covered her side almost from breast to waist.

“What did he shout?” she asked.

“Who?”

“Mitia.”

“Sergei is needling him.”

“You should stop it.”

“Why? Let him learn to answer.”

“He cannot.”

“Then let him learn.”

Marka looked toward the stern, but the piled timber and fog concealed the men.

“He sounded strange.”

“He always sounds strange. Like a door squeaking in an empty house.”

“You are cruel.”

Silan’s beard moved with his smile.

“And you love me.”

She lowered her eyes.

“That is why I know.”

He drew her nearer. Against his strength she became pliant; her shoulder fitted beneath his chin, and when he bent to kiss her, she received the kiss first gravely, almost sadly, then with a warmth that made him utter a low pleased sound.

“There,” he whispered. “Is that cruelty?”

“Yes.”

“Then I’ll be cruel again.”

She pushed at him, smiling now.

“Enough. They may come.”

“Let them.”

“Sergei has eyes like a thief.”

“He has nothing to steal here.”

Silan said this with such simple possession that Marka’s smile faded. She touched his beard and drew her fingers through it.

“Am I yours?” she asked.

“Whose else?”

“His, before the law.”

“Paper law.”

“And before the Church.”

“Church law.”

“And before God?”

At that Silan’s face grew serious. He was not irreligious. On saints’ days he attended service, gave candles, fed beggars when they approached him respectfully, and feared thunder, bad dreams, and death. But his religion, like his labour, belonged to the earth. God for him was a great master who loved courage, understood a man’s necessities, punished weakness, and could be appeased by repentance when the work of living was done.

“Before God,” he said slowly, “we are sinners.”

Marka shivered.

“You say it calmly.”

“Should I lie?”

“No.”

“I know sin when I see it. You were married to my son. I take you. That is sin.”

“Then give me up.”

His arm tightened until she caught her breath.

“Say that again.”

She smiled faintly.

“I knew you would do that.”

“Give you up! For what? So that Mitia may look through you as through window glass? So that you may freeze in his room while he warms his soul? No.”

“Then you choose sin.”

“I choose you.”

Beyond the awning the water struck a projecting log: slap-slap, slap-slap. Somewhere behind them Mitia coughed. Marka’s face stiffened.

Silan felt it.

“You pity him?”

“I don’t know.”

“You pity yourself.”

“Yes.”

“That is more honest.”

She rested her head upon his chest. Through his shirt she could hear his heart, steady and strong. That sound had first conquered her. After the silent misery of Mitia’s room, after his evasive eyes and gentle explanations, Silan’s loud breathing, laughter, anger, and powerful heartbeat had seemed to her not merely masculine but merciful. He desired her; and for a woman who had begun to believe herself ugly, accursed, or somehow less than a woman, desire had been a hand pulling her from deep water.

“You ought not to have married us,” she said.

“I know.”

“You forced him.”

“I thought marriage would straighten him. A bent sapling must be tied to a stake.”

“I was the stake?”

“You were a fine girl. Strong. Sensible. Your father owed me money; I knew your people; you worked well. What more was needed?”

“Love.”

Silan grunted.

“You talk like Mitia.”

“No. He used that word to keep me away. I use it because I came to you.”

He considered this, then nodded.

“You are right.”

“Did you never think of me for yourself?”

“At that time my old woman was alive.”

“She was dying.”

“She was alive.”

“And if she had died before the wedding?”

“I would have married you.”

Marka raised herself to see his face.

“Truly?”

“Why should I lie?”

“You never said.”

“What use now?”

The question opened before them a glimpse of another life, so near in imagination and so completely lost that both were silent. Had Silan’s wife died half a year earlier; had he noticed Marka not as a useful bride for his son but as a woman fitted to himself; had Mitia resisted more firmly; had Marka refused—then the same passion which now crawled furtively beneath canvas and darkness might have stood crowned before the altar, blessed by priest and parents, welcomed with bread, salt, songs, and drunken cries. Their children might have run openly through Silan’s yard. Neighbours who now spat after Marka would have praised her strong arms and obedience.

The difference between honour and disgrace had been no wider than a few months, a mistaken arrangement, a dead woman’s last breaths.

Silan frowned.

“I was a fool.”

“You are never a fool.”

“I was then. I saw Mitia growing thinner, always with books and prayers, afraid of girls, afraid of vodka, afraid even of slaughtering a chicken. I thought: marry him to Marka. She has life enough for two. She’ll shake him awake.”

“I tried.”

“I know.”

“He looked at me as if I were tempting him to murder.”

“He is rotten with thoughts.”

“He was kind.”

“Kindness without strength is sour milk. It feeds no one.”

“He never struck me.”

“That is not much praise.”

“He did not curse.”

“Nor bless you as a husband.”

Marka’s mouth twisted.

“No.”

Silan lifted her chin.

“Do not remember it.”

“How can I not? The first night—”

“Do not.”

“I had been frightened all day. The women laughed and whispered. Your wife was already ill, but she helped unpin my veil. She said, ‘Bear him sons, Marka. This house needs noise.’ Then they left me. Mitia came in. He sat on the chest and would not look at me.”

Silan’s jaw hardened.

“He asked whether I was tired. I said no. He asked if I wanted water. I said no. Then he began—oh, those words! Soul, truth, conscience! At first I thought he was shy. I went to him. He stood up as if a snake had touched him.”

“He’ll answer for that.”

“He said I was beautiful.”

“What use was that?”

“He said it was not my fault. That was worse. Not my fault! As if I had a disease.”

Silan stroked her hair, but his eyes were fixed upon the darkness.

“I should have thrashed him until he had sense.”

“You did.”

“Not enough.”

“No beating could make him love me.”

“Love! Again love.”

“Yes, love. You say it justifies us. Why should it not have mattered to him?”

Silan’s broad face became impatient. He had accepted the contradiction in himself, but disliked hearing it named.

“A husband’s duty is one thing. What is between us is another.”

“Why?”

“Because it is.”

“That is not an answer.”

“It is the only answer life gives. One horse pulls, another lies down in the harness. Do you ask why? Beat the lazy one or cut it loose.”

“Mitia is not a horse.”

“No. A horse is useful.”

She pulled away.

“Do not speak so.”

Silan looked at her with narrowed eyes.

“You defend him often tonight.”

“I defend myself. If he is nothing, then what am I? I was married to nothing, rejected by nothing, ruined because nothing would touch me.”

“You are mine. That is what you are.”

Again the possessive force of his voice soothed and frightened her. She leaned back into his arms.

From the stern came Mitia’s cry—“Be silent!”—thin but piercing. Marka started. Silan raised his head, and the muscles in his arm swelled under her hand.

“What are they doing?”

“Sergei is a fool.”

“Go and see.”

“No. If Mitia cannot manage Sergei’s tongue, he can swallow it.”

They listened. The words did not carry clearly, only the tones: Mitia’s high, broken vehemence, Sergei’s mutter, and then Silan’s own shout asking what was the matter. After Sergei replied, quiet returned.

Marka crossed herself.

“He will do something.”

“Who?”

“Mitia.”

“He never does anything.”

“He may throw himself into the river.”

Silan was silent.

The possibility entered the shelter and sat with them. Neither looked at the other. The lantern flame bent and straightened, bent and straightened, making the shadows of the ropes crawl upon the canvas like black serpents.

At length Marka whispered:

“If he died, what would happen?”

Silan’s hand ceased moving upon her shoulder.

“What happens when any man dies? They wash him, bury him, divide what he leaves.”

“You know what I mean.”

“Yes.”

“Could we marry?”

“After a proper time.”

“How long?”

“A year, perhaps.”

“A year!”

“Would you have people say we killed him for the wedding feast?”

“They say worse now.”

“Let them talk. Talk does not break bones.”

“It breaks other things.”

Silan sighed. For all his contempt of opinion, he understood its practical force. A man might despise the village and still need labourers from it, buy fodder from it, borrow horses, find godparents, witnesses, customers, and sons-in-law. Even strength lived among people; only the dead were wholly independent.

“We could go away,” he said.

“Where?”

“Downriver. Beyond Saratov, perhaps. Or east. Sell the house, sell the remaining timber, buy land where no one knows us.”

“Begin again?”

“Why not?”

“You are fifty-five.”

“And stronger than Sergei.”

She smiled and put her hand upon his chest.

“That is true.”

“I’ll get you sons yet.”

Her smile deepened, but sadness remained behind it.

“And then?”

“We work. We raise them. We give to the poor. Build a chapel, maybe. A man can atone.”

“For this?”

“For any sin, if his heart does not lie.”

Marka gazed toward the black river.

“If Mitia died by his own hand, could we atone?”

Silan’s brows drew together.

“He must not do that.”

“Why?”

“Suicides are buried outside consecrated ground.”

“You care for that?”

“He is my son.”

The words were blunt, almost angry. Marka lowered her head.

“Yes.”

“I don’t wish him damned.”

“But you wish—”

She stopped.

Silan’s eyes fixed upon her.

“What?”

“You wish he were gone.”

He pushed her away enough to examine her face.

“Do you?”

She did not answer.

“Speak.”

The domineering note in his voice compelled her as always.

“Yes.”

The word was scarcely audible.

“Gone where?”

“Dead.”

The lantern hissed. A drop of condensed moisture fell upon the flame, and for a moment darkness filled the shelter. Marka gave a little cry and clutched Silan. The flame recovered, weak and blue at its base.

“You pray for that?” he asked.

She covered her face.

“Sometimes.”

“Marka.”

“I am wicked. I know.”

“Do you pray?”

“At night. I say: ‘Lord, forgive me. Take him gently. He is ill, he suffers, he wants to leave this world. Take him, and let us live.’ Then I am afraid and pray for his health. But afterward I hear him cough, and I think—soon. Perhaps soon.”

Silan’s face had grown grave. Yet beneath his gravity something responded to her confession—not horror alone, but hope. He saw, against his will, the future she had named: Mitia lying peaceful beneath a cross; a year passing; a wedding in a distant village; Marka beside him without shame; children; fields; broad daylight instead of canvas and fog. He hated himself a little for seeing it so clearly, and because he was accustomed to mastering whatever opposed him, he turned the hatred upon his son.

“He is half dead already,” he muttered. “Never had health. His mother spoiled him, kept him by the stove, filled him with saints’ lives. At ten he spoke of monasteries. At fifteen he refused meat on fast days and fainted in the field. What use is such a man?”

“He feels everything.”

“That is his disease.”

“Perhaps we are the disease.”

Silan made an impatient gesture.

“Must three people die because one cannot live? You were withering. I was burning. He stood between us like a fence and called the fence holy.”

“He did not put himself there. You did.”

“I know!” Silan struck his fist against a timber. The lantern jumped. “How many times must I say it? I made a mistake. A man turns into the wrong channel; does he smash the boat out of reverence for the mistake? No. He finds deep water.”

“And Mitia?”

“He must find his own.”

“He says he will go to the Caucasus.”

Silan stared.

“He told you?”

“Long ago.”

“To those mad brethren?”

“Yes.”

“They’ll put ideas in him against the Tsar, against priests, against property. He’ll be arrested.”

“He wants to go.”

“He will not.”

“Why keep him?”

“Because I will not have a son of mine wandering with sectarians.”

“You despise him, yet you hold him.”

“He bears my name.”

“And I bear his.”

Silan’s eyes flashed.

“Not in my heart.”

She looked at him steadily.

“That does not change the papers.”

He swore under his breath and reached for her, but she rose and stepped beyond the shelter.

The fog was beginning to lift. The eastern sky remained cloudy, yet its darkness had thinned from black to pearl-gray, and a pale radiance lay upon the river. Marka stood barefoot on the wet logs, holding the awning rope. The current lifted strands of her hair and pressed her blouse against her body. She looked young, strong, and sorrowful.

Silan followed.

“Come back. It’s cold.”

“No.”

“You’ll be wet through.”

“I want air.”

“There is air under the awning.”

“Not enough.”

The phrase, echoing Mitia without her knowledge, irritated him.

He took off his coat and put it around her shoulders.

At the stern the figures of Mitia and Sergei had become visible through the dissolving vapor. They stood close to the long sweep. Sergei’s head was bent, and the usual angular liveliness had left his body. Mitia looked small beside him, almost transparent in the growing light.

“What if he goes?” Marka asked.

“He won’t.”

“What if he does?”

“I’ll fetch him back.”

“Why?”

Silan was silent.

“Let him go,” she urged. “Give him money. Let him find his brethren. Then we could go away too.”

“Still married.”

“Far away, no one would know.”

“God would know.”

She looked at him in surprise.

“You say love justifies us.”

“I say it makes the sin worth bearing. I don’t say there is no sin.”

“What is the difference?”

“The difference is a man must know the weight he carries.”

Marka wrapped the coat more tightly around herself.

“And if the weight crushes someone else?”

Silan followed her gaze to the stern.

“He should grow stronger.”

“Can grass grow strong under a cartwheel?”

“He is not grass.”

“To you he is.”

The clouds overhead began to break. Their lower edges kindled faintly, first ash-white, then yellow. The immense gray wall which had all night barred the river opened into drifting gates. Through them appeared spaces of tender green sky, pure and remote. The wooded bank emerged from mist; every birch trunk shone silver, every pine branch carried trembling drops. A field beyond the trees glimmered emerald, and over it the vapor lay in long rosy bands.

Day broke gradually.

Nature, indifferent during the dark hours or seeming to brood upon them, now thrilled, quickened, and smiled. The river changed beneath the growing light. Its leaden surface became blue, then purple, then gold where the east touched it; every small wave raised a bright edge and hurried away rejoicing. Dew upon the ropes flashed like diamonds. Birds called from the bank, tentative at first, then in a multitude of clear voices. A fish leaped and fell with a silver splash. Smoke rose straight from an unseen cottage, and the smell of damp earth came over the water.

Silan breathed deeply. Dawn restored his faith in strength. The clearing sky, the broad river, the raft laden with his timber, the woman warm beneath his coat—all seemed to confirm him. Life moved forward. It did not apologize; it did not ask permission of the weak or halt before old mistakes. It burst through cloud, bred in mud, sang in throats, swelled in muscle and breast. To live was to desire, labour, possess, suffer, and go onward.

He put his arm around Marka.

“Look,” he said. “Would you throw that away?”

She leaned against him.

“No.”

“Nor I.”

“Even for salvation?”

“We’ll earn salvation afterward.”

“How?”

“By living honestly when we can. We’ll help people. Feed beggars. Raise children well. No cheating. No cruelty.”

She glanced toward Mitia.

“No cruelty?”

Silan’s face hardened, then softened again.

“I’ll speak to Sergei. He shall leave the boy alone.”

“And you?”

“What of me?”

“Will you leave him alone?”

“He is my son.”

“That is not an answer.”

“It is all I have.”

They stood watching the sunrise. Silan bent and kissed the side of her neck. Marka closed her eyes. The light spread over them boldly now, revealing what darkness had concealed: his gray-threaded beard against her black hair, his thick arm about her waist, her full lips parted in response. Their tenderness was sinful, selfish, and alive; and because it was alive, it possessed a beauty which made judgment difficult.

At the stern, Sergei saw them.

He glanced quickly at Mitia, hoping the pale man was looking elsewhere. But Mitia too had seen.

For a moment his face showed nothing. Then he lowered his eyes to the water.

Sergei cleared his throat.

“Sun’s coming.”

“Yes.”

“It’ll be warm.”

“Yes.”

“We’ll make the landing by noon if the current holds.”

Mitia did not answer.

Sergei moved nearer the edge, placing himself awkwardly between Mitia and the lovers, though there was no way his lean body could hide them across the length of the raft.

“Tea soon,” he said. “I’ll boil it strong.”

Mitia’s mouth twitched—not quite a smile, not quite pain.

“You need not be kind from fear.”

“I’m not afraid.”

“You are.”

“Of you? I could tuck two of you under my arm.”

“Not of me. Of what is in me.”

Sergei looked down into the brightening river.

“Perhaps.”

The admission cost him effort.

Mitia turned his pale face toward the opening sky. In the dawn his tears had dried to shining tracks. He appeared exhausted, but his eyes were calm.

“Do you believe God can lead a man out?” he asked.

“Out of what?”

“Sin. A house. Himself.”

Sergei scratched his beard.

“I believe a man needs legs.”

“And if his legs are weak?”

“Then someone may carry him a little.”

Mitia studied him with surprise.

Sergei became embarrassed.

“Not me, mind! I’ve work enough. I mean—someone. Those brethren of yours, perhaps.”

“My father will not let me go.”

“You are twenty-seven.”

“He will beat me and lock away the money.”

“Earn your own.”

“With what strength?”

“There are ways. Keep accounts for a merchant. Read letters. You read well, don’t you?”

“Yes.”

“Then use what God gave, even if it’s only eyes and a gloomy face. A widow might pay you to read holy books.”

Mitia looked again toward the bow. Silan and Marka still stood together, luminous in the sunrise.

“He will always stand in the way.”

Sergei followed his gaze.

“No man stands forever.”

Mitia shivered.

“Do not say that.”

“I meant—move round him. Like the snag. You don’t break the snag or ask it to be kind. You put the sweep over and find water.”

For the first time that night Mitia smiled. It was a small, sorrowful smile, but it changed his whole face and made Sergei aware of the youth buried beneath illness.

“You have preached to me now,” Mitia said.

“Don’t insult me.”

They were silent again, though the silence had altered. It no longer suffocated Sergei. Daylight filled it with birds, running water, and the soft hiss of mist lifting from the wet timber.

At the front, Silan released Marka and strode toward the stern. The raft trembled under his steps. He came immense and red in the morning light, his beard like fire, his eyes clear from wakefulness and desire.

“Sergei!” he shouted. “Get the kettle on. We’ll take tea.”

“Aye.”

“And mind the bend. There are shoals beyond that point.”

“I know.”

Silan stopped before Mitia.

The two looked at one another: the father overflowing with life, the son worn thin by the effort of defending an invisible law. Between them lay Marka’s body, the authority of the Church, the mockery of men, blood kinship, property, fear, pity, and hatred—ropes knotted so tightly that no hand could discover which end to pull.

“What was your yelling about?” Silan asked.

“Nothing,” said Mitia.

“He was taken with a cough,” Sergei interposed.

Silan glanced at him, sensing the lie.

“A cough has words now?”

“This one does.”

“Keep your jokes for work.”

Sergei lowered his eyes.

Silan turned back to his son.

“You’re white as flour.”

“I am tired.”

“Sleep after tea.”

“I will.”

“And pull when I say pull. We’re nearing a bad channel.”

“Yes, father.”

The obedience pleased Silan and angered him at once. He wanted resistance so that he might conquer it, yet Mitia’s submissiveness denied him the dignity of battle.

He seized the steering sweep.

“Look ahead!” he commanded.

All three looked.

Ahead, the Volga widened magnificently beneath the risen sun. Islands floated in blue haze; sandbanks shone like gold; distant villages lifted white bell towers above green fields. The clouds, defeated, withdrew in purple masses toward the west. The river seemed to promise freedom because no wall was visible upon it, though every current had its channel and every raft was bound to move where the water carried it.

Marka remained at the bow, Silan’s coat around her shoulders. She crossed herself before the bright east.

Her lips moved.

Perhaps she prayed for forgiveness. Perhaps she prayed for Mitia’s health. Perhaps, beneath both prayers, there remained the dark petition she had confessed: that the frail obstruction might soon be taken gently away, leaving the strong to live.

Mitia watched her, then looked beyond her toward the far south, where the river vanished in light and where, immeasurably farther, rose the mountains and the imagined brotherhood of pure men. He saw no path from the raft to that distant life. Yet he held the vision stubbornly within him, a small flame guarded by thin hands against wind.

Silan planted his feet and leaned upon the sweep.

“Port!” he roared.

Sergei and Mitia threw their weight beside his. The great blade resisted, bent, and slowly yielded. Water boiled around it in green and golden whorls.

“Harder!”

They pulled.

The raft groaned like a living creature under torment. Logs strained against ropes; chains clinked; the river slapped and gurgled along its sides. Marka clung to a post at the bow, her red blouse bright beneath the dark coat. Sergei bared his teeth with effort. Mitia coughed, stumbled, recovered, and pulled again.

Together, though each desired a different shore, they turned the raft into the channel.

Then the current took them.

Behind, the fog closed over the night they had passed through; ahead, the sun blazed upon fathomless water. Silan shouted, Marka prayed, Sergei busied his tongue no more, and Mitia, pale beneath the immense morning sky, held fast to the sweep while the Volga bore them all relentlessly onward.

Every clock in Mara Venn’s shop stopped at 4:17 on the morning her father disappeared.

His coat was gone. So were his boots.

On the workbench lay a brass key Mara had never seen before.

Beside it, written in her father’s narrow handwriting, was a message:

Do not wind the clock beneath the river.

For eleven years, Mara obeyed him.

She grew skilled enough that people crossed the city to consult her. She could coax a heartbeat from a rusted chronometer or diagnose a broken escapement by sound alone. But the clocks that had stopped the night her father vanished resisted every repair.

She kept them in the back room, hands frozen at 4:17.

The brass key remained in a locked drawer.

Then, on a rainy afternoon in November, a boy brought her a clock from the river.

COLLECTION AT MIDNIGHT.

The boy stepped back. “I should go.”

“No,” Mara said. “You should tell me everything you saw.”

It was not much.

Finn sold newspapers near the railway station. That morning he had gone to the river to retrieve a coin dropped through the railings. Beneath the old bridge, the water had withdrawn farther than he had ever seen, exposing a door of green metal. Beyond it, steps descended underground.

He had followed them to a round chamber where hundreds of clocks were embedded in the walls. Some ran backward. Some had too many hands. One had whispered his name.

A man stood in the middle of the chamber, separated from Finn by what looked like a sheet of rain, though they were indoors. He pushed the iron clock-house through the watery curtain and gave Finn his instructions.

“Did he say anything else?” Mara asked.

Finn nodded. “He said you’d need the key.”

At six that evening, Mara closed the shop.

At seven, she took the brass key from the drawer.

By eight, the river had fallen low enough to reveal the door.

Finn insisted on coming.

“You delivered the clock,” Mara told him. “Your part is finished.”

“He knew my name.”

“Who did?”

“The clock in the wall.”

“All the more reason to stay away.”

But Finn crossed his arms with the rigid determination unique to children who have spent too much time surviving adults.

“If Tuesday disappears, I’ll miss getting paid. Mr. Hob says he only pays on Tuesdays.”

Mara studied him, then handed him a lantern.

“Stay behind me.”

The green door opened with the brass key.

Beyond it, stone steps spiraled into darkness. The air smelled of wet iron and extinguished candles. As they descended, the sounds of the city faded until Mara could no longer hear the motorcars on the bridge or the river moving over stone.

At the bottom waited the chamber Finn had described.

It was larger than the shop above and perfectly round. Clocks covered the walls from floor to ceiling. There were sundials untouched by sunlight, hourglasses filled with blue ash, wooden cuckoo clocks, marine chronometers, and glass spheres in which tiny stars wheeled through artificial skies.

Their combined ticking made the air vibrate.

In the center stood a black pedestal. On it rested a clock with a face like the moon.

“Is that the one?” Finn whispered. “The clock beneath the river?”

“I think so.”

The moon-faced clock had a keyhole in its side.

Mara’s warning returned with absolute clarity.

Do not wind the clock beneath the river.

Above the pedestal hung a brass plaque:

BELLWEATHER MUNICIPAL RESERVE  
AUTHORIZED HOURS ONLY  
THEFT WILL BE COLLECTED

Finn read slowly. “Reserve of what?”

“Time,” Mara said.

He laughed once, hopefully. When she did not, he moved closer to her.

On the far side of the chamber, the air shimmered. A curtain of rain appeared where there had been only stone. Behind it stood a man in a dark coat.

He had aged.

His hair, once brown, was almost white, and his face was cut with deep lines. Yet Mara knew the slope of his shoulders and the careful way he held his hands, as if some invisible mechanism might break between his fingers.

“Father,” she said.

He lifted his palm to the watery barrier.

Mara crossed the chamber before caution could stop her. She pressed her hand against his, separated by a cold surface that yielded like rain but would not let her through.

“You’re alive.”

“Yes.”

“Where have you been?”

“Here.”

“For eleven years?”

“For me, somewhat longer.”

Anger rose so quickly that it surprised her.

“You left me.”

“I tried not to.”

“You wrote six words.”

“They were the only six I had time for.”

“You had eleven years.”

“Not where I was.”

The clocks ticked around them.

Elias looked at the iron clock-house under Mara’s arm. “You brought the collector.”

“It came looking for me.”

“It came looking for the debt.”

“What debt?”

“Mine.”

He glanced upward, as though he could see the city through the stone.

“Years ago,” he said, “before you were born, Bellweather suffered a fire. It began in a textile warehouse and spread across the eastern quarter. Three thousand people were trapped between the flames and the river.”

Mara knew of the Great Fire. Everyone did. A sudden rainstorm had extinguished it before dawn, though the night had begun under a cloudless sky.

“I found this place by accident,” Elias continued. “The city’s founders built it. They discovered that time does not always pass evenly. A joyful summer afternoon may vanish in a breath. A minute beside a deathbed can feel endless. Those differences leave traces. Seconds, minutes, sometimes entire days accumulate like silt.”

“In the reserve,” Mara said.

He nodded. “The founders learned to collect those fragments. They could release stored time during emergencies. One extra hour allowed the trapped families to reach the river before the fire crossed the district.”

“You did that?”

“I wound the clock.”

Mara touched the brass key in her pocket.

“The rainstorm,” she said.

“Came an hour later. The official histories never noticed the difference.”

“What was the price?”

“The reserve must balance. An hour borrowed is an hour owed.”

Finn frowned. “That doesn’t sound much.”

“An hour from every citizen,” Elias said, “including those not yet born. Each year, the collector chooses a day and takes its payment in small pieces. A missed train. A forgotten conversation. A moment when someone enters a room and cannot remember why.”

“That happens all the time,” Finn said.

“Exactly.”

Mara looked at the clock-house. “Then why does it say one hour outstanding?”

“Because I interrupted the collection eleven years ago. I believed the debt had long been paid. It had not. The collector had been taking interest.”

“How much?”

“By my calculations, Bellweather had repaid nearly three hundred years.”

The ticking seemed suddenly predatory.

“I tried to stop it,” Elias said. “At 4:17 that morning, I entered the reserve and reversed the municipal clock. The collector trapped me outside ordinary time.”

“And now?”

“Now it intends to take a full day from the city.”

“Tuesday.”

“Not the memories of Tuesday. Tuesday itself.”

Finn hugged the lantern closer. “What happens if a day disappears?”

“No one knows. People may wake on Wednesday believing nothing is wrong. Or the missing day may leave a wound. Events without causes. Children born before they are conceived. Letters answered before they are written.”

Mara removed the key from her pocket.

Elias shook his head sharply. “No.”

“You told Finn I would need it.”

“To open the door, not wind the clock.”

“You also told me not to wind it. That is not the same as saying it can’t help.”

“Mara, listen to me. The municipal clock releases time, but it does not create it. If you turn that key, the reserve will demand an exchange.”

“What kind of exchange?”

“A day for a day.”

The iron collector clicked in her arms.

Another strip of yellow paper emerged.

THREE HOURS UNTIL COLLECTION.

Finn read it and muttered, “It’s bad manners to count.”

Mara walked around the pedestal, examining the moon-faced clock. The mechanism was exquisite. Her father’s influence showed in several repaired gears, but the original construction was far older. Along the lower edge of the case, almost hidden by tarnish, ran an inscription:

TIME FREELY GIVEN BEARS NO DEBT.

“What does this mean?” she asked.

Elias came as close to the barrier as he could. “I never understood.”

“Perhaps because you were trying to cheat the machine.”

“I was trying to save the city.”

“So am I.”

“No. You are trying to save me.”

For a moment she was eight again, sitting beneath his workbench while he repaired a music box. He had always known when she was lying, especially to herself.

“Yes,” she said.

His expression softened.

“I am sorry.”

“That is not enough.”

“I know.”

“You don’t get to vanish for eleven years and become noble because you had a reason.”

“I know.”

“You left me to wonder if I had driven you away. If you had fallen in the river. If you were alive somewhere and simply chose not to return.”

“Mara—”

“I hated you.”

“I know.”

“I still do, a little.”

“You should.”

She put her hand against the barrier again.

“And I missed you every day.”

Elias closed his eyes.

Behind Mara, Finn cleared his throat.

“I think the clock wants something.”

The symbols on the moon-faced dial had begun to glow. A feather. A flame. An eye. A crown. A boat. One after another, pale light filled them until only the final symbol remained dark.

It was shaped like an open hand.

Mara looked again at the inscription.

Time freely given bears no debt.

“The fire,” she said. “You borrowed one hour for everyone, without asking them.”

“There was no time to ask.”

“So the reserve treated the hour as a loan.”

“Yes.”

“What if it had been a gift?”

Elias frowned.

Mara turned to Finn. “How many people live in Bellweather?”

He shrugged. “Lots.”

“About two hundred thousand. If each person willingly gave a fraction of a second, we would have more than a day.”

“How do you ask an entire city at midnight?” Elias said.

Mara looked at the walls of clocks.

“You use the proper instrument.”

She knelt beside the pedestal and opened its lower panel. Inside, gears moved through a nest of brass wires. Some vanished into the floor, spreading beneath the city like roots.

The public clocks, she realized. The reserve was connected to every clock maintained by the municipality: railway clocks, factory clocks, school clocks, the great clock in the tower of City Hall.

She removed a screwdriver from her coat.

“Mara, what are you doing?”

“Sending a message.”

“With a clock?”

“People trust clocks. That is why clocks are dangerous.”

She worked quickly.

At eleven fifty-five, every public clock in Bellweather stopped.

The railway clock froze above the platforms. Factory clocks halted in rooms smelling of oil and cotton dust. The City Hall clock ceased with its minute hand pointing straight up.

Then they began to strike.

Not the hour. Not any hour.

They struck a pattern Mara had tapped into the municipal mechanism: four slow bells, one quick bell, seven slow bells. The time at which her father vanished. The minute in which the city’s debt had last been challenged.

People woke.

Windows opened. Night workers put down their tools. Policemen stepped into the streets. In taverns, hospitals, kitchens, and signal boxes, the citizens of Bellweather looked toward the nearest clock.

Through every dial came Mara’s voice.

She did not know how the reserve carried it. Perhaps her words traveled along the wires. Perhaps time itself had learned to speak.

“My name is Mara Venn,” she said, “and the city owes an hour.”

She told them about the fire.

She told them about the reserve beneath the river and the years stolen in forgotten fragments. She told them that, at midnight, Tuesday would be taken unless the city repaid its debt.

“I cannot prove this,” she said. “By morning, you may think it was a dream. But if you believe me, place your hand on a clock. Give one second freely. Think of that second and let it go.”

She hesitated.

“A second is enough to say I love you. It is enough to step off a curb, pull a trigger, catch a falling glass, or change your mind. A second is not nothing. I have lost eleven years one second at a time, and I know their value.”

She looked at her father behind the rain.

“I would not ask if there were another way.”

Throughout Bellweather, hands touched clocks.

An old woman placed her palm against the watch of her dead husband. A nurse touched the clock above a hospital door. The night watchman at City Hall climbed six flights of stairs and laid both hands on the great mechanism.

Some people laughed and went back to bed.

Some cursed the interruption.

Some gave more than a second.

Finn put his hand on the moon-faced clock.

“I’ll give a minute,” he announced.

“You don’t have to.”

“I know. That’s the point, isn’t it?”

Mara placed her hand beside his.

The clock was warm.

She thought of a summer morning in her father’s shop. Sunlight on brass. The smell of tea. Elias guiding her small fingers as she fitted a gear into place.

Never force the mechanism, he had told her. Listen for what it needs.

She gave the memory whole.

Pain passed through her—not physical pain, but a clean absence. She still knew she had learned clockwork from her father, yet the morning itself was gone. No sunlight. No tea. No warmth of his hand.

The final symbol on the dial began to shine.

All around the chamber, clocks accelerated. The noise swelled until individual ticks became a rushing wind. The watery barrier rippled.

The collector on the floor unfolded.

Its iron walls opened like jointed legs. The copper door split into a mouth crowded with gears. From inside came a sound like thousands of people gasping as they woke from sleep.

A final paper strip curled from the roof.

PAYMENT REJECTED.

“Why?” Finn shouted.

Elias stared at the collector. “It cannot take freely given time. But it can refuse to count it.”

The hands of the municipal clock spun toward midnight.

Mara tore open the collector’s back. Beneath the iron case, gears snapped at her fingers. She saw no balance wheel, no mainspring—only a hollow space into which darkness poured.

“It was never collecting the debt,” she said.

“What?” Elias called.

“It was feeding.”

The collector lunged.

Finn swung the lantern. Glass shattered against iron, splashing flame across the machine. It recoiled, gears shrieking.

Mara seized it with both hands and lifted it onto the pedestal.

“Mara, stop!” her father cried.

She drove the brass key through the collector’s open back and into the keyhole of the moon-faced clock.

The two mechanisms locked together.

The clock began to wind.

The force nearly broke her wrist. She held on, turning the key as the collector twisted beneath her hands.

Eleven years of stolen fragments burst from the machine.

They filled the chamber as light: blue, gold, white, the deep red of sunset. Within the radiance Mara glimpsed lost moments. A woman remembered why she had entered a room. A man on a train recovered the name of his childhood dog. A child found the ending of a dream. Thousands upon thousands of abandoned seconds flew upward through the stone.

The clock reached midnight.

Its bell rang once.

The curtain of rain collapsed.

Elias fell forward onto the chamber floor.

The collector gave a small, disappointed click.

Then it became an ordinary iron box.

For several moments, no one moved.

At last Finn peered over the pedestal. “Is it Wednesday?”

“Not yet,” Mara said.

“Good. I’ve never liked Wednesdays.”

Elias pushed himself up. His hands shook.

Mara stood a few feet away, suddenly uncertain. Rescuing a father was easier than greeting one.

He looked older outside the barrier. Smaller, too.

“I cannot return what you lost,” he said.

“No.”

“I cannot ask you to forgive me.”

“No.”

“I can come home, if you’ll let me.”

Mara considered the man before her: the father she remembered, the stranger he had become, the missing shape around which she had built her life.

“You can rent the room above the shop,” she said. “For now.”

A faint smile crossed his face.

“Fair.”

“And you will not touch the accounts. Or the regulators. Or any clock older than the monarchy.”

“Understood.”

“And you owe me eleven birthday presents.”

“Twelve,” Finn said. “Interest.”

Mara looked at him.

He shrugged. “Seems fair.”

They climbed the stairs before dawn.

The river had risen behind the green door, sealing the reserve beneath dark water. Across Bellweather, clocks resumed their motion. Tuesday arrived exactly where it belonged.

In the weeks that followed, people argued about what had happened. The newspapers called it a citywide electrical disturbance, though half the affected clocks had never used electricity. Clergymen called it a warning. Scientists called it mass suggestion. The mayor appointed a committee, which ensured that nothing useful was discovered.

Some citizens remembered Mara’s message clearly. Others retained only a dream of bells.

But the people of Bellweather became more careful with their time.

Factory owners shortened Tuesday shifts by one minute. Trains waited an extra second before departure. At noon, the old woman with her husband’s watch sat in the park and did nothing at all.

Finn began working at Venn & Daughter after school. He proved terrible at polishing brass but gifted with delicate springs. Elias rented the upstairs room and obeyed most of Mara’s rules.

The clocks that had stopped at 4:17 began running again.

All except the tiny silver watch Mara wore around her neck.

No matter what she tried, its hands remained fixed. In time she stopped trying to repair it.

Some moments, she learned, were not broken merely because they did not move.

Years later, when people asked why the clockmaker on Bellweather Street kept a stopped watch close to her heart, Mara would smile and say it told a kind of time that ordinary clocks could not measure.

Then she would return to her work, listening to the thousand small heartbeats around her, each one spending its seconds, each one keeping a promise no machine could make.
